input: Why software will be bought per request, not per seat
title: The Seat Is No Longer the Atomic Unit of Software
report:
# The Seat Is No Longer the Atomic Unit of Software
*Per-usage overtook per-user as the most common SaaS pricing model in Q2 2026. Here is what founders should actually change, and where keeping the seat is still the right call.*
A seat that asks an AI to summarize 1,000 documents costs the vendor roughly [1,000 times what a seat summarizing one document costs](https://sfailabs.com/guides/the-end-of-the-per-seat-ai-pricing-model). That single sentence is why the seat is losing its place as the default unit of software.

It is not a fashion cycle. It is a COGS line.

## The mechanism, not the trend

Once a software company carries per-token cost of goods, a flat seat fee is effectively a bet that the buyer will not use the product. a16z's argument, cited in Causo's H1 2026 pricing report, is that because "every API call, every token processed, adds to their cost structure," the per-seat unit is [no longer the atomic unit of software](https://hub.causo.ai/guides/h1-2026-saas-pricing-report).

The logic gets sharper when the primary user is not an employee. When AI agents do the work, the value of a platform [stops being a function of how many employees have access](https://www.informationweek.com/software-services/how-ai-agents-broke-traditional-saas-pricing).

> Once you carry a per-token COGS line, a flat seat fee is a bet that your customer will not use your product.

## The numbers point one way, at different speeds

The adoption figures overlap rather than agree, and I would present them as a range rather than a fact.

1. Causo's mix puts roughly [60% of SaaS companies on some usage-based component](https://hub.causo.ai/guides/h1-2026-saas-pricing-report), with 46% hybrid usage-plus-seat and 15% largely usage or pay-as-you-go.
2. Kyle Poyar's survey of 230-plus software companies puts pure usage-based adoption at [38% in 2026, up from 27% in 2023](https://valueaddvc.com/blog/the-death-of-the-annual-saas-contract-how-usage-based-pricing-is-taking-over), with 61% running hybrid base-plus-meter and pure per-seat shrunk to roughly 8%.
3. Vertice's quarterly tracking shows per-usage rising to [36.5% in Q2 2026 to lead all models, with per-user down to 32.4%](https://www.vertice.one/insights/saas-pricing-models).

IDC forecasts that [70% of software vendors will have refactored away from pure per-seat pricing by 2028](https://valueaddvc.com/blog/the-death-of-the-annual-saas-contract-how-usage-based-pricing-is-taking-over). Different samples, different definitions, same direction.

## Per-seat fails in two opposite directions

For vendors, the exposure is margin. Usage variance across an AI user base is effectively unbounded once heavy users start running [agentic workflows](https://sfailabs.com/guides/the-end-of-the-per-seat-ai-pricing-model). If consumption per user varies by 10 times across your base, [usage or hybrid is the honest model](https://leanware.co/insights/usage-based-vs-seat-based-pricing-ai-products); seats only hold when per-user consumption is tight and bounded.

For buyers, the failure mode is paying for access nobody uses. Slack Business+ at $15 per user per month works at medium-to-high engagement but [breaks when 30% of seats are inactive and cannot be removed](https://saastruecost.com/guides/per-seat-vs-usage-based-pricing-explained/), inflating the bill by the same 30%. HubSpot Sales Hub Professional at $100 per user per month suits active teams of 10 to 200, and becomes wildly inefficient with part-time SDRs.

## The counter-evidence I would not ignore

Here is the finding that should slow anyone down. In Futurum's 2H 2026 survey of enterprise software decision-makers, per-seat ranks *last* for core software at 12.6%, behind consumption at 28.9% and outcome at 22.2%. But for AI functionality billed as a separate line item, per-seat ranks [first at 42.3%](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/the-pricing-split-why-core-software-and-ai-cant-share-one-commercial-model/), ahead of consumption at 36.6%.

The same buyers want metering for core software and predictability for AI. Bain finds about [one in five AI-native software companies still relies mostly on per-seat licensing](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-pricing-a-reality-check-on-effort-usage-and-outcomes/), often supplemented with usage entitlements.

So the seat is being displaced as the primary unit, not eliminated. The surviving seat products, Slack, Notion, Figma, are [gaining pricing power, not losing it](https://hub.causo.ai/guides/h1-2026-saas-pricing-report).

## Pick your meter by who carries quality risk

Bain separates three meters that most commentary blurs together: [effort-based](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-pricing-a-reality-check-on-effort-usage-and-outcomes/) (tokens, compute, agent hours), output-based (summaries, drafts, records updated), and outcome-based (an issue resolved, fraud recovered, revenue collected).

The split test is simple. Under output pricing you get paid regardless of whether the output creates value. Under outcome pricing, payment depends on business results.

The market sits in the middle. Among companies adding a hybrid AI meter, only about [10% use outcome meters, versus roughly 35% effort and 55% output](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-pricing-a-reality-check-on-effort-usage-and-outcomes/). Outcome pricing has a real home in customer support, where a resolved conversation is observable and attributable: Intercom Fin at [$0.99 per resolution](https://hub.causo.ai/guides/h1-2026-saas-pricing-report), HubSpot Breeze Customer Agent at [$0.50 per resolved conversation](https://valueaddvc.com/blog/pricing-strategy-for-ai-products-seat-based-usage-based-or-value-based). Beyond support it is messier: marketing attribution is disputed, HR decisions span systems and people, and engineering productivity is hard to measure consistently.

Bain also notes that most so-called usage-based pricing is in practice [capacity-based with overages](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-pricing-a-reality-check-on-effort-usage-and-outcomes/), and that capacity is emerging as the preferred model because it gives buyers a predictable budget and vendors stable revenue.

## The hybrid trap, and how to price around it

Hybrid compounds when it is misread, because you pay per seat for access *and* per unit for consumption inside it. Datadog Infrastructure at $15 per host per month plus $0.10 per million log events is fine at low ingest, but custom metrics and log indexing tiers can push a [$40,000 contract to $400,000 in an incident month](https://saastruecost.com/guides/per-seat-vs-usage-based-pricing-explained/). The OpenAI API at $2.50 per million input tokens on GPT-4o can take a prototype from $200 a month to $40,000 in production through long-context retrieval and reasoning chains.

Forecasting discipline is the mitigation: pull the last 90 days of raw daily usage, compound the observed month-over-month trend, add a [20% buffer for incident spikes that routinely run 5 to 10 times normal volume](https://saastruecost.com/guides/per-seat-vs-usage-based-pricing-explained/), and negotiate a committed-use discount at 70% of the projection so overage bills at the discounted rate.

## Metering is an engineering project, not a price-list edit

Metered pricing moves complexity from the price list into the pipeline. Implementing it requires [precise metering, flexible pricing logic and billing automation](https://lago.ghost.io/architect-billing-systems/) to prevent revenue leakage.

Every billable action generates an event, and the ingestion layer has to be durable, because [services fail and messages get dropped in distributed systems](https://abaxus.software/blog/2025-06-01/metered-usage-billing-complete-guide-to-saas-revenue-optimization/). Store the smallest defensible unit with customer, org, request and metric fields plus an [idempotency key so the same call is not counted twice](https://zyrox.io/blog/api-usage-billing-for-developer-products/). Webhooks arrive with at-least-once semantics, so [deduplicate on that path too](https://lorbic.com/designing-a-usage-based-billing-pipeline-for-saas/).

Get this wrong and you under-bill quietly. Nalpeiron, which sells metering infrastructure, reports homegrown metering commonly [under-bills by 4 to 7%](https://nalpeiron.com/zenmeter/usage-based-pricing/infrastructure/) from missed events and race conditions, and estimates 6 to 12 months to build in house. Treat those figures as directional, given the source.

## What I would actually do

Futurum's recommendation is blunt and I agree with it: run [two pricing architectures](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/the-pricing-split-why-core-software-and-ai-cant-share-one-commercial-model/), moving core software toward consumption or outcome structures while separately billed AI defaults to per-seat or a capped, budgetable variant. Futurum also expects pricing optionality to become a [shortlist gate by Q4 2026](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/the-pricing-split-why-core-software-and-ai-cant-share-one-commercial-model/), screened like a security certification rather than negotiated.

Instrument requests. Choose the meter that matches who carries quality risk. Offer a capped variant to buyers who need a budget line they can defend.

Which unit are you pricing on right now, and could you produce an accurate per-request cost for your top ten accounts this week?
## Key takeaways
- AI cost-to-serve scales with requests, so a seat running 1,000 AI summaries costs the vendor roughly 1,000 times a seat running one, per SFAI Labs.
- Per-usage became the single most common SaaS pricing model at 36.5% in Q2 2026 while per-user slipped to 32.4%, according to Vertice.
- Buyers are split by product type: per-seat ranks last for core software at 12.6% but first for separately billed AI at 42.3% in Futurum's 2H 2026 survey.
- Only about 10% of hybrid AI meters are outcome-based, versus roughly 35% effort and 55% output, and Bain finds capacity-with-overage emerging as the preferred practical model.
- Metering is an engineering commitment: durable ingestion, idempotency keys and webhook deduplication are prerequisites, and Nalpeiron reports homegrown systems commonly under-bill by 4 to 7%.
